bach-invention-8.title: Invention No. 8 in F major, BWV 779
bach-invention-8.subtitle: J. S. Bach, c. 1723 · two-part invention for keyboard · complete
bach-invention-8.tempoText: Allegro (no marking in Bach’s copy) · practice ♩ = 100

sections.label: I
sections.name: Part 1 · F major to C major

sections.label: II
sections.name: Part 2 · C major, G minor, D minor

guide.text: The subject: an F-major arpeggio that leaps up (F–A–F–C–F). Bach builds the whole Invention from this one bar and the run that follows it.
The left hand copies the right hand exactly, one bar later and one octave lower: a canon. While it copies, the right hand plays a new running line that has to fit against it.
A sequence: the right hand’s broken-third figure (A–C–B♭–C) drops a third each bar (A, then F, then D), and the left hand copies each bar one bar later.
B♮ appears for the first time: it is the leading note of C major, so the music is heading for a new key.
Both hands trade running sixteenths toward C. Follow the bass in bar 11: D–E–D–C, then G down to low G, the dominant of C.
Cadence in C major, the dominant key: the end of Part 1. In the same bar the left hand starts the subject in C, so the hands swap jobs.
Now the right hand follows the left: the canon again, with the hands reversed.
E♭ and F♯ sound together, a diminished-seventh colour that pulls the music toward G minor.
The subject and its run in G minor, passed between the hands.
B♭ against C♯ in the right hand: another diminished-seventh sound, this time leading to D minor.
The subject in D minor (D–A–F–D–A–F): the farthest the piece travels from home.
A falling sequence: each bar repeats the same shape one step lower while the bass moves in steady eighths.
The bass jumps between octaves (D, then C) as the harmony moves toward B♭ major.
The bar-4 sequence returns, with the subject in the left hand in B♭ major (bar 26) and the broken thirds falling bar by bar.
A C-major arpeggio with B♭ added (C7): the dominant seventh that leads home to F.
Final descent: both hands run down in sixteenths, the right hand echoing the run from bar 2.
The closing cadence: the bass falls from C to F and both hands land on an F-major chord.

chopin-prelude-7.title: Prelude in A major, Op. 28 No. 7
chopin-prelude-7.subtitle: Frédéric Chopin, 1839 · piano · complete

guide.text: A pickup E, then the rhythm of the whole piece: a dotted figure (C♯–D) and two repeated chords. The chord is E7 (D–G♯–B over E), the dominant of A.
The answer: A-major chords over the bass A. Each two-bar unit is a question (E7) and an answer (A).
The same question and answer again, with the melody a little higher. Count the mazurka-like lilt: long–short, then two even chords.
Third phrase, still on E7.
The surprise: the melody leaps to C♯6 over an F♯7 chord (F♯–A♯–C♯–E), the most colourful harmony in the piece.
F♯7 resolves to B minor (bar 13); then E7 (bar 14) brings the music back toward home.
Final A-major chords. The piece ends quietly after just sixteen bars.

tchaikovsky-old-french-song.title: Old French Song, Op. 39 No. 16
tchaikovsky-old-french-song.subtitle: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, Album for the Young, 1878 · piano · complete

guide.text: The melody climbs G–A–B♭–C to D and repeats it, like a singer. The left hand plays a gentle accompaniment of held notes and chords.
The phrase rises to E♭, then falls to a cadence on G with F♯, the leading note of G minor (bar 7).
The whole melody again, ending firmly in G minor.
A new idea: the melody steps up on repeated notes (G, B♭, C, A) while the bass moves C–G–C–D.
The climax of the middle section, up to F5 (bar 22), then a half cadence on D major (bar 24).
The song returns as at the start.
A new ending: the melody falls through E♭ and D to G, and the piece closes softly in G minor.

tchaikovsky-wooden-soldiers.title: March of the Wooden Soldiers, Op. 39 No. 5
tchaikovsky-wooden-soldiers.subtitle: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, Album for the Young, 1878 · piano · complete

guide.text: A crisp D major chord, a rest, then a little turn B–A♯–B: the toy soldiers step off. The rests matter as much as the notes; play every note short.
The same two bars again, so the listener learns the tune.
The melody climbs D–E–F♯ in chords toward the top of the phrase.
Steps back down and stops on an A chord, while the left hand taps A A A A like a drum.
The opening four bars return note for note.
The climb again, but this time the left hand jumps down to D4.
The phrase now cadences in A major (G♯ is the clue), and the drumming A moves down an octave.
Middle section: the march moves to A, and B♭ (a flat sixth) darkens the little turn. Same rhythm, new colour.
The B♭ turn again, over a D minor chord in the left hand.
The melody steps up A–B–C♯ while the bass climbs with E♯ and F♯: the harmony is heading to B minor.
A falling phrase over B and E, and the left hand walks down E–D–C♯–B.
The middle section begins again, with the same B♭ turns.
The rising line again, with E♯ pushing upward.
This time the phrase closes firmly on A, and the left hand walks up A–B–C♯ to lead back home.
The march returns exactly as it began.
The opening bars once more; listen for the thinner chord in bar 43.
The climb to F♯5, with the bass moving to B for a fuller cadence.
D♯ leans up to E, then the march ends on a single D: soldiers halt.

joplin-entertainer.title: The Entertainer
joplin-entertainer.subtitle: Scott Joplin, 1902 · “A Rag Time Two Step” · piano · complete

guide.text: Introduction: both hands play the opening figure in octaves, D–E–C–A–B–G, then settle on a G-major chord (the dominant of C).
The famous tune. The right hand’s melody lands between the beats (syncopation) while the left hand keeps a steady “oom-pah”: bass note, chord, bass note, chord.
The phrase repeats and turns toward G major (D7 in bar 11).
The opening phrase again, this time heading back to C.
First ending: repeat the strain from bar 5.
Second ending: rising chords lead into the second strain.
Second strain: thick right-hand chords and a new syncopated tune, still in C major. Listen for the left hand walking up and down between chords.
The strain continues and closes in C.
First and second endings of the second strain.
The first strain returns, without its repeat.
The trio (third strain) moves to F major: one flat in the key signature. The tune has a new, lighter rhythm.
The trio’s second phrase, ending in F.
First and second endings of the trio.
A four-bar transition back to C major.
Fourth strain: a new tune in C with chromatic neighbour notes (C♯–D, D♯–E).
The fourth strain’s second phrase, closing toward C.
First ending repeats the strain; the second ending finishes the piece on a C-major chord.

beethoven-fur-elise.title: Für Elise, WoO 59 (Bagatelle in A minor)
beethoven-fur-elise.subtitle: Ludwig van Beethoven, 1810 · piano · complete

sections.label: C
sections.name: Episode in A minor over a pedal

guide.text: The famous opening: E and D♯ rock back and forth, a half step apart. D♯ is the leading note of E, so the melody circles E before falling to A.
The left hand answers with broken chords: A minor (bar 2), E major with G♯ (bar 3), A minor (bar 4). The right hand fills each gap with a short rising figure.
The same phrase again. This time bar 7 approaches the cadence through C instead of G♯.
First ending: go back to the start (bar 0).
Second ending: after the repeat, skip bar 8 and play this bar. Its rising B–C–D leads into a brighter section.
An interlude in C major: E–G–F–E, D–F–E–D, C–E–D–C. Each bar is the same shape a step lower (a sequence); the bass outlines C, G, A minor.
The hands share the E–D♯ figure across two octaves (up to E6 in bar 14), sliding back to the main theme.
The main theme returns.
First ending: repeat from bar 10 (the C-major interlude and the theme).
Second ending: the left hand plays B♭, the first flat in the piece. The music is turning to F major.
Episode in F major: a singing, more decorated melody over steady broken chords (F major, B♭ major, C7 over F).
The melody climbs chromatically (C–D–D♯–E) toward C major.
Fast 32nd-note figures in C major: the right hand flickers around G while the left hand plays short chords. Practise slowly, then speed up.
The E–D♯ figure returns, repeated like a trill, leading back to the theme.
The main theme, the C-major interlude and the main theme again, exactly as at the start (without the repeats).
A darker episode: the left hand repeats a low A in sixteenths (a pedal note) under tense chords, including the diminished seventh C♯–E–G–B♭ (bar 62).
The bass climbs D, D♯, E beneath the chords before falling back to A.
The pattern starts again; then the pedal moves up to B♭ (bars 73–75) and B (76), raising the tension.
Resolution: an A-minor chord over C, then E major (E–G♯–B).
An A-minor arpeggio sweeps up three octaves to E7, the highest note in the piece.
A chromatic scale tumbles down from B♭6, every half step, back to the E–D♯ figure.
The main theme and the interlude one last time. The piece ends quietly on A.

beethoven-symphony-7-allegretto.title: Symphony No. 7 in A major, Op. 92 — II. Allegretto
beethoven-symphony-7-allegretto.subtitle: Ludwig van Beethoven, 1812 · full orchestra · complete movement (clarinets in A, horns in E and trumpets in D shown at sounding pitch)

guide.text: A single wind chord (oboes, clarinets, bassoons, horns) opens and closes the movement like a curtain.
The theme, in the low strings only (violas, cellos, basses): the rhythm long–short–short, long–long repeats in every bar while the harmony changes slowly underneath.
Variation 1: the second violins take the theme an octave higher; the violas and cellos add a new singing countermelody.
Variation 2: the first violins have the theme, the countermelody moves up, and the woodwinds join in.
Variation 3: the whole orchestra plays the theme fortissimo, with trumpets and timpani on the rhythm.
The music thins out to the first violins, preparing a change of key.
Middle section in A major (three sharps): clarinets and bassoons sing a warm melody while the violins ripple in triplets and the bass keeps the old rhythm.
A sudden fall back to A minor: a descending scale, then brass and timpani hammer the rhythm.
The theme returns in the low instruments while flutes, oboes and violins decorate it in quick notes.
Fugato: the violins start the theme as a fugue subject and the other strings enter one by one, imitating it.
The full orchestra plays the theme loudly once more.
The A-major melody returns, shorter this time.
Coda: fragments of the theme pass between the strings and the woodwinds, growing quieter, and the movement ends with the opening wind chord.

beethoven-ode-to-joy.subtitle: Ludwig van Beethoven, 1824 · melody in D major, the key of the finale

source.label: Melody as it appears in the finale; checked against the Mutopia Project setting

excerpt.label: the complete theme with its repeat, melody line

guide.text: The melody moves almost entirely by step (F♯–G–A, A–G–F♯–E…), which is why a crowd can sing it. The dotted quarter and eighth in bar 4 give the phrase its little lurch, and it stops on E: a question.
The same phrase with a different ending: it falls to D, the home note. An answer.
The middle phrase starts with a repeat sign. It circles around E, and the quick eighth notes F♯–G add a skip in its step.

Beethoven’s surprise: the melody drops to a low A, then the next phrase’s F♯ arrives a beat early, tied over the barline. That early note is a syncopation, and it is what makes the tune feel like it leans forward.
The answer phrase from bars 5–8 returns and ends on D. The repeat sign sends you back to bar 9, so the theme is 24 bars long as the orchestra plays it.

sections.name: Coda: the melody in the bass

guide.text: Beethoven’s instruction over the first bar: play the whole piece very delicately, with the dampers raised (the sustain pedal down). The right hand plays triplets, three notes to each beat, outlining C♯ minor, while the left hand’s bass octaves step down C♯, B, A, F♯, G♯.

The melody enters on top: a G♯ repeated in a dotted rhythm (long, short, long), like a slow, quiet signal. It sits on the highest note of each triplet, so the pianist plays melody and accompaniment with one hand and voices the top note louder.
A surprise: G naturals turn the music to E minor. The melody hovers around G while the bass steps down E, D, C, B, heading for B minor.
The melody rocks between B and C, a half step that sounds like a sigh, then turns toward F♯ minor.
In F♯ minor the melody climbs step by step, C♯, D♯, E, over rising triplets.

A long G♯ in the bass, the dominant of C♯ minor, holds underneath while the triplets climb to D♯6, the highest point of the movement. Listen for the tension: the bass will not move until the melody comes home.
The triplets sink back down, still over the G♯ pedal, until they settle low in the left hand.
The melody returns in C♯ minor, as at bar 5. This time it turns to brighter E major, then reaches a D-major chord (bar 50), a half step above home.
The half-step sigh from bars 15–18 returns, now C♯ to D, and the phrase closes with a full cadence in C♯ minor (bars 57–59).
Coda: the dotted G♯ melody moves down into the bass, under the triplets. Mute the right hand to hear it alone.
The triplets sink to the bottom of the piano and the movement ends on two quiet C♯-minor chords. Beethoven writes “attacca subito il seguente”: go straight on to the next movement.

guide.text: A light minuet-like tune in D♭ major: the same notes as C♯ major, written with flats so they are easier to read. Listen for the touch: a slurred pair of chords, then short, detached ones (the dots in bars 2 and 3). Liszt called this movement “a flower between two abysses.”
The same tune again, now doubled in octaves, ending firmly in D♭ major.
The second half begins with C♭ (a B natural on the piano), a flat seventh that tilts the music toward G♭ major for a moment.
The opening tune returns in octaves and closes in D♭. The repeat sign sends you back to the upbeat before bar 17.
The Trio: the left hand holds a low A♭ while the right hand plays octaves tied across the barline, so the accents land on the wrong beat. Repeat once.
The second half of the Trio keeps the tied octaves and the low pedal notes.

The Trio ends on D♭; repeat its second half once. Then D.C. al Fine: back to the start of the Allegretto and play it once more without repeats, stopping at Fine (the end of bar 36). The player follows the jump for you.

beethoven-moonlight-3.title: Piano Sonata No. 14 in C♯ minor, Op. 27 No. 2 (“Moonlight”) — III. Presto agitato
beethoven-moonlight-3.subtitle: Ludwig van Beethoven, 1801 · piano · complete movement

guide.text: The storm the first movement held back. The right hand races up a C♯-minor arpeggio in sixteenth notes over a pounding bass. This bar is the lead-in: the repeat at the end of the exposition goes back to bar 2, and the first ending (bar 65) plays the lead-in again.

First theme: each rising arpeggio ends in two loud, short chords (sforzando, sf). The same idea climbs through C♯ minor, G♯ major, C♯ major and F♯ minor: the C♯-minor arpeggio that drifted quietly through the first movement, now racing.
The right hand plays a rising line against a repeated high G♯ while the left hand answers below, all over a G♯ bass. The fermata in bar 14 holds the music on the dominant chord.
Transition: the arpeggios start again but turn through A♯ and D♯, toward a new key.
Second theme, in G♯ minor: a singing melody over steady sixteenth notes in the left hand. Bars 25–28 repeat it louder, in octaves.
Octaves step down while the left hand keeps up its sixteenths: a sequence, the same pattern moved lower each time.
Sixteenth-note scales over an A-major chord. In G♯ minor, A major is the Neapolitan chord, a half step above home; it makes the cadence in bars 41–42 sound even stronger.
Closing theme: repeated chords in eighth notes, quiet and nervous, then loud and higher in bars 49–52.
Over a G♯ pedal, the right hand holds long notes and the music winds down to the end of the exposition.
First ending: the lead-in arpeggio again, then back to bar 2 to repeat the exposition.
Second ending and the start of the development: the first theme’s arpeggios in C♯ major, then F♯ minor.
The second theme, now in F♯ minor. From bar 77 it moves into the left hand while the right hand takes over the sixteenths, and it travels through D major and G major.
A long G♯ pedal in the bass (bars 88–100), the dominant, with quiet chords above. The music gets softer and softer (pp in bar 102) so the return of the first theme hits harder.
Recapitulation: the first theme returns in C♯ minor, up to the fermata in bar 116.
The second theme comes back in C♯ minor, the home key. In a minor-key sonata form, this is the tragic turn: the theme that was in G♯ minor now stays in the home key.
The Neapolitan scales again, now over D major (a half step above C♯).
The closing theme and its long-note ending, now in C♯ minor.
Coda: instead of stopping, Beethoven brings back the first theme’s rising arpeggios a third time.
Arpeggios that pile up into diminished-seventh chords, each held under a fermata: the most dissonant moment in the sonata.
The second theme returns, first in the left hand under racing sixteenths (bars 168–171), then in right-hand octaves.
Broken chords sweep up and down the keyboard through F♯ minor, D major and a diminished seventh, landing on a C♯-minor chord over G♯.
A chromatic scale, every half step, climbs from the left hand into the right hand.

A trill on A, then a cadenza that tumbles down from G♯5 to G♯2. Beethoven writes the run in small notes, to be played freely; here it is spelled out in even sixteenths so the player can follow it, in a bar of its own.
Adagio: two low octaves, F𝄪 and G♯, played slowly. The player keeps the main tempo, so try lowering the speed for these two bars, or count them slowly yourself.
Tempo I: quiet repeated chords over a C♯ pedal in the bass.
The last arpeggios rush down the keyboard, and the sonata ends with loud C♯-minor chords.

sections.name: Horn call, then the second theme (E♭ major)

sections.label: Ch
sections.name: Chords traded between winds and strings

guide.text: The four-note motto: short, short, short, long. G–G–G–E♭, held under a fermata, then F–F–F–D, held longer. Strings and clarinets play it in unison, so you can’t tell yet what key it is in.

The motto passes from the second violins to the violas to the first violins, each entry stacked on the last, quiet at first and building to the fermata in bar 21. Mute every part but the strings to hear the hand-off.
The full orchestra plays the motto fortissimo, ending on another fermata.
The motto again, quiet, passed through the strings, then a crescendo to fortissimo chords. Count how many bars still use the short-short-short-long rhythm.
The horns, alone and fortissimo: the motto rhythm stretched into a call (B♭–B♭–B♭, E♭, F, B♭) that announces the new key, E♭ major.
Second theme in E♭ major: a gentle, smooth melody in the violins, then the woodwinds. Underneath, the cellos and basses keep tapping the motto rhythm, so the first theme never really goes away.
The music builds to a fortissimo climax with the trumpets.
Closing section: the motto rhythm returns under long held notes, ff, in E♭ major. The repeat sign at bar 124 sends you back to bar 1 to hear the whole exposition again.
Development: the horns and clarinets play the motto fortissimo, B♭–B♭–B♭–G, and the strings answer. Fermata.
The motto is passed from instrument to instrument in imitation, quietly at first, through F minor and other keys, then grows into a long crescendo to fortissimo.
The horn call from bar 59, broken into pieces and traded between the violins and the full orchestra.

Beethoven strips the horn call down to single half-note chords and alternates them between the winds and the strings, getting quieter (pp by bar 221). Look at the score: whole bars of rests in one group while the other plays.
A sudden fortissimo outburst, then the quiet chords again, then a crescendo that leads straight into the return of the motto.
Recapitulation: the motto, fortissimo, with fermatas as at the start, and the motto passed through the strings again. This time the oboe plays a slow line on top of it.

The oboe cadenza: the orchestra stops on a fermata chord, and the oboe plays a short, slow, sad solo (Adagio) alone. It lasts only a moment, but nothing like it happened in the exposition. It is written here as a bar of its own; the player keeps the main tempo, so the solo goes by faster than a real oboist would take it.
The music picks up where it left off and rushes on toward the second theme.
The horn call, now played by the bassoons. In C major the call needs notes that horns in E♭ could not play in Beethoven’s time (they had no valves), so he gave it to the bassoons.
Second theme in C major, the home key’s bright major side.
The full orchestra drives to a fortissimo close in C major, but the movement is not over.
Coda: hammered chords and the motto bring the music back to C minor. A coda this long works like a second development.
The horn call in the bassoons and cellos while the first violins play a new running line in eighth notes against it.
A new marching tune in the violins, in quarter notes, over long notes in the bass.
The motto, fortissimo, tossed back and forth between the winds and the strings with the trumpets and timpani.
The opening motto with its fermatas one last time, then a quiet echo in the woodwinds and strings.
Fortissimo C-minor chords end the movement.

bach-prelude-c-major.title: Prelude in C major, BWV 846
bach-prelude-c-major.subtitle: J. S. Bach, The Well-Tempered Clavier, Book 1 (1722) · complete

guide.text: C major. Every bar of this piece is one chord played as the same broken pattern: a held bass note, a second held note, then three notes repeated in the right hand.
D minor seventh over C (ii⁴₂). Only the notes change; the pattern stays the same.
G seventh with B in the bass (V⁶₅): the dominant, pulling back to C.
C major again. Bars 1–4 are a complete progression: home, away, tension, home.
A minor with C in the bass.
D seventh over C. F♯ appears: it is the leading note of G, the key Bach is heading for.
G major with B in the bass.
C major seventh over B: the bass is walking down step by step.
A minor seventh.
D seventh, the chord that leads to G (the dominant of the dominant).
G major: the music has arrived in the dominant key.
C♯ diminished seventh over G. C♯ wants to rise to D, so this chord leans toward D minor.
D minor with F in the bass.
B diminished seventh over F: A♭ adds a darker colour.
C major with E in the bass: home again, but not yet settled.
F major seventh over E.
D minor seventh.
G seventh: the dominant.
C major, now in a lower register.
C seventh: adding B♭ turns C into a chord that leads to F.
F major seventh.
F♯ diminished seventh (F♯–A–C–E♭): the bass has risen a half step to F♯.
A diminished seventh sound (B–D–F–A♭) over A♭ in the bass, with C held over from the bar before.
G seventh. From here to bar 31 the bass stays on G: a dominant pedal that builds tension before the end.
C major over the G pedal (a 6/4 chord).
G–C–F over G: a suspended dominant (G7sus4).
G seventh.
F♯ diminished seventh over the G pedal: the most dissonant moment of the pedal.
C major over G again.
G7sus4 again: the same harmonies as bars 25–27, repeated to stretch the waiting.
G seventh, the last dominant chord over the pedal.
C seventh over a low C: the bass finally lands on C and stays there (a tonic pedal).
F major over C: the pattern changes for the first time, a rising and falling arpeggio.
G seventh over C, a last moment of tension above the tonic pedal.
The final C-major chord.

bach-cello-prelude.title: Cello Suite No. 1 in G major, BWV 1007 — Prélude
bach-cello-prelude.subtitle: J. S. Bach, Köthen, c. 1720 · solo cello · complete movement

sections.label: I
sections.name: Home: G major over the open G string

guide.text: The open G string (G2) sounds at the start of every half bar: a pedal note. Above it the harmony moves G → C → D7 → G, all spelled out as broken chords on one instrument.
Leaving home: C♯ (bar 6) belongs to an A7 chord, which pulls toward D major in bar 7.
E minor (bar 8), a running scale (bar 9), then D major (bar 10).
G♯ is the leading note of A: the music turns to A minor in bar 12.
D♯ leads to E minor; bar 14 runs down the scale to the open G string.
Back toward G: D7 over F♯ (bar 15), G7 (16), C over G (17) and D7 over G (18).
A long scale falls from B3 to D2, the lowest note so far.
The bass sinks chromatically, C♯ then C, under the same rocking pattern.
The line climbs: a D-major arpeggio rises to D4 (bar 22) and pushes on to E♭4 in bar 24, the highest tension yet.
A low D anchors the harmony while the patterns turn back toward A and D.
Two long falling scales, each one starting a step lower.
Bariolage: the open A string (A3) alternates with a moving line, so one cello sounds like a melody plus a ringing pedal note.
Over the open D string the top line climbs chromatically, one half step at a time, from F♯3 to F♯4: the most famous build-up in the piece.
Arrival: high G4 rings out over D, then A and F♯ tensions (bars 40–41) prepare the final cadence.
The final G-major chord: G2, B3 and G4 together.

mozart-sonata-facile.title: Piano Sonata No. 16 in C major, K. 545 (“Sonata facile”) — first movement
mozart-sonata-facile.subtitle: W. A. Mozart, 1788 · piano · complete movement

guide.text: First theme in C major over an Alberti bass (the left hand breaks each chord into low–high–middle–high). The melody is simple: C–E–G, then a turn back down.
Scales: each bar is a rising scale starting one step lower (A, G, F, E), while the left hand holds chords.
C♯ (bar 9) and F♯ (bar 10) lead to a cadence in G major, the new key.
The left hand plays alone: C♯–D–C♯–D, a restless figure that prepares the second theme.
The second theme in G major: a gentle falling figure over a shimmering left hand.
Arpeggios fall in steps, each bar one note lower.
A closing idea with a trill, approaching G through A minor and D.
Codetta: G-major arpeggios close the exposition. The whole exposition repeats.
The development begins with the codetta’s idea in G minor (B♭).
C♯ and then D minor: the music moves through new keys.
Sequences in A minor: falling patterns over a bass that steps down, then B♭ turns toward F major.
The recapitulation surprises the listener: the first theme returns in F major, not C.
The scales again, a step lower than before.
The bass climbs and the music returns to C major for the cadence.
The second theme, now in C major (the home key).
Falling arpeggios and the trill idea, all in C.
Codetta in C major. The development and recapitulation repeat together.

guide.text: The tune everyone knows as “Twinkle, Twinkle”: C up to G, A, then back to G. Under it the left hand plays a simple bass: low C, then a second voice of E, F, E against a repeated middle C.
The answer steps down the scale, F–E–D, to C, and the bass steps down with it (D–B, C–A, F–G). The little dotted rhythm in bar 7 leans into the cadence. Play bars 1–8 twice (repeat signs).
The middle: G–F–E–D over a held-down G in the bass every second beat. A pedal note like this keeps the harmony waiting.

The same step-down again, now decorated: in bar 15 three quick grace notes (F–E–D) curl around the E. In bar 16 the left hand splits into two voices, C–B above a held G, and stops on a G chord: unfinished.

The opening returns with its bass and finishes on C, with one more grace-note turn in bar 23. Bars 9–24 are repeated. Mozart keeps this exact shape (A–A–B–A) and this bass in all twelve variations while changing everything else.

sections.label: B
sections.name: “Each morning I get up with the sun”

guide.text: The trick of the song: a seven-note figure (F–A♭–G–F–B♭–B♭, rest) in a bar of eight eighth notes. Because it is one eighth short, each repeat starts one eighth earlier in the bar, so the accents keep sliding against the beat. Underneath, the left hand rocks between B♭7 and A♭ on every beat, keeping a steady pulse the melody can fight against.
The figure stops on a long low B♭: the rhythm catches its breath.
The same sliding figure a fourth higher (B♭–D♭–C–B♭–E♭), over E♭7 and D♭ chords, landing on E♭.
A contrasting section with longer notes: “Each morning I get up with the sun”. Bar 12 (“Start a hopping, never stopping”) bounces on repeated Gs.
The sliding figure returns, low then high, exactly as before.
A new climbing phrase, “Oh, how I long to be the man I used to be”, reaching the high F. The courtesy natural on D in bar 26 cancels the D♭ heard earlier.
One last statement of the figure, turning to end on E♭.
First ending: repeat the refrain.
Second ending: the final E♭.

guide.text: The rising pickup figure: E♭–F–G–B♭–C–E♭ in dotted rhythms, climbing an octave to reach for the “somebody”.
Three falling steps, each a step lower (F–E♭–D, E♭–D–C, D–C–B♭): a sequence that sounds like a sigh. Underneath, the left-hand bass creeps down by half steps: A♭, G, F♯, F, E♮.
The phrase reaches up to E♭5, then drops an octave and settles on G and F, “someone who’ll watch over me”.
The A section again, ending this time on E♭, the home note.
The bridge stays high: D and E♭ alternate, then F–E♭–D repeats, each bar a slight variation. B♮ in bar 22 is a leading note to C minor colours.

guide.text: The hook: a rest, then F tied across the beat. Almost every phrase starts after beat 1 and leans across the beat with a tie: syncopation you can see.
The same opening, answered by the high E♭ and a cadence on B♭: “Who could ask for anything more?”
The A section again, ending on a long B♭.

The bridge (“Old Man Trouble”): the melody holds on D, then C, while the harmony moves through D7, G7, C7 and F7, each chord leading to the next (a chain of dominants). E♮ in bar 18 belongs to the D7 and C7 colours. In the left hand you can hear the bass step through D, G, C and F.
The A section returns.

Gershwin stretches the last phrase by two bars: the melody climbs to F and repeats “Who could ask for anything more?” This is why the original refrain is 34 bars, not the 32 bars of jazz “rhythm changes”.

chopin-prelude-4.title: Prelude in E minor, Op. 28 No. 4
chopin-prelude-4.subtitle: Frédéric Chopin, 1839 · piano · complete

guide.text: A melody of almost only two notes, B and C, over soft repeated chords. Listen to the chords, not the tune: in each bar one note of the chord slips down a half step.
The melody steps down to A and B while the chords keep sinking chromatically, so the harmony never settles.
The melody finally moves (bar 9) and reaches a half cadence on B major with A added (B7, bar 12): a question.
The opening returns, but now the chords sink faster and the melody pushes upward (bar 16).
The climax: a deep B octave in the bass and the melody’s cry up to C6, the only loud moment.
The energy drains away; the melody hovers on E and F♯ over a slowly falling bass.
A chord with B♭, then silence: Chopin stops before the final cadence.
The cadence: B7 chords (with D♯) resolve to E minor, played very softly.

chopin-prelude-20.subtitle: Frédéric Chopin, 1839 · piano · complete

sections.name: Soft phrase over a falling bass

guide.text: Fortissimo chords, one per beat, like a funeral march: C minor, F minor, G7, C minor.
The same rhythm in A♭ major: A♭, D♭, E♭7, A♭.
G7, then C7 leading to F minor, and back to C minor.
D7 and G, twice: a half cadence on G, the dominant.
Suddenly soft. The bass walks down C–C–B–B♭ while the chords change above it.
The bass keeps falling, A–A♭–G–F: a chromatic descent.
Cadence: E♭–F–B–C in the bass, then A♭–D♭–G–C, home to C minor.
Bars 5–8 again, even more quietly, like an echo.
The final C-minor chord, held.

mozart-turkish-march.title: Piano Sonata No. 11 in A major, K. 331 — Rondo alla turca
mozart-turkish-march.subtitle: W. A. Mozart, 1783 · piano · complete third movement

sections.label: B
sections.name: B: the answer (C major, then A minor)

guide.text: The refrain in A minor: a circling sixteenth-note figure (B–A–G♯–A) climbs in steps, C–D–C–B–C, then E–F–E–D♯–E. The left hand plays “oom-pah-pah” chords.
The tune turns over an E-major chord (the dominant) and closes back in A minor. This whole section repeats.
The second idea, in C major, then A minor: short phrases of thirds in the right hand over a bouncing bass.
The refrain returns and closes in A minor; bars 8–24 repeat.
The famous march in A major (three sharps): loud octaves in the right hand and repeated broken chords in the left, imitating Turkish military bands.
An episode in F♯ minor: running sixteenths with E♯ and B♯, the leading notes of F♯ minor and C♯ minor.
A bright tune in A major, running up and down in sixteenths.
Back to the F♯-minor sixteenths, ending with chords that lead into the march.
The march again.
The A-minor refrain and its second idea return exactly as at the start.
The march once more.
Coda in A major: the left hand rolls drum-like arpeggios (shown as grace notes) under ringing chords.
Repeated high C♯s over the drumming bass, then the chords again.
The final A-major chords, played forte.

mozart-eine-kleine-1.title: Eine kleine Nachtmusik, K. 525 — first movement
mozart-eine-kleine-1.subtitle: W. A. Mozart, 1787 · string quartet or string orchestra · complete movement

guide.text: The “rocket” theme: all four parts play the same G-major arpeggio together (in unison and octaves), then answer with D7.
The first violin sings a graceful line while the second violin plays fast repeated notes (written as tremolo in the printed score) and the bass holds G.
Soft and light: a short new idea, passed between the parts.
A crescendo with repeated notes in all the instruments.
The music settles in D major (bars 22–24); then the bass climbs to A, the dominant of D, and holds it (bars 26–27) to prepare the second theme.
The second theme, in D major: elegant and quieter, with rests between short phrases.
The closing theme: repeated notes and a little turn, stated twice.
Codetta in D major. The whole exposition repeats.
The development opens with the rocket theme in D major.
The closing theme travels through new keys: C major, A minor and D, then an E♭ in the bass adds a dark colour.
A rising scale passage leads back to G.
Recapitulation: the rocket theme and first theme in G, as at the start.
The transition, changed so that it stays in G.
The second theme, now in G major.
The closing theme in G.
The coda begins with the codetta material and short scale figures.
The rocket figure one last time and repeated G-major chords to finish.

vivaldi-spring-1.title: “Spring” (La primavera), Op. 8 No. 1 — first movement
vivaldi-spring-1.subtitle: Antonio Vivaldi, The Four Seasons, published 1725 · solo violin and strings · complete movement

guide.text: The ritornello (“the returning part”): the whole orchestra plays a bright tune in E major, loud.
The same phrase repeated softly, like an echo.
The second half of the ritornello, again loud then soft, ending in E major.
Birdsong: the solo violin and two orchestral violins trill and chirp on high repeated notes. Vivaldi wrote “Canto degli uccelli” (song of the birds) in the score.
A short return of the ritornello.
The streams: soft, flowing sixteenth notes in the violins, as the sonnet says “the springs flow with sweet murmurs”.
The ritornello again, now moving to B major.
Thunder: fast repeated notes (tremolo) and rising scales in the whole orchestra.
Lightning: the solo violin flashes up and down in fast arpeggios over pulsing chords.
The ritornello in C♯ minor: the storm has darkened the music.
The birds come back after the storm: the solo violin trills high over a held C♯ in the bass.
The ritornello returns to E major.
A last solo passage with running notes.
The final ritornello closes the movement in E major, soft at the end.

guide.text: The hypnotic opening ostinato: a low bass note on beat 1, then a rich, unresolved major-seventh chord on beat 2. Satie alternates between Gmaj7 (G–B–D–F♯) and Dmaj7 (D–F♯–A–C♯).
The melody enters softly with an arching line (F♯–A–G–F♯–C♯–B–C♯–D–A). Notice how the melody floats over the bar lines with quiet, unhurried restraint.
A single note, F♯4, is held for four whole measures while the bass keeps rocking between G and D. This radical stillness was decades ahead of ambient and minimalist music.
The opening melodic phrase returns, re-establishing the gentle 3/4 dance lilt.
The melody steps upward to C♯5 and F♯5 before settling onto a long held E4, suspended over shifting bass notes (F♯2, B1, E2, D2).
A new rising phrase begins: A–B–C, climbing through E–D–B to D5. The chords turn more chromatic and questioning as the left hand sustains D in the bass.
The phrase climbs again (E–F♮–G–A–C–D) with natural F introducing an enigmatic, modal twist before peaking on D5.
The first cadence begins with a high G5 descending through F♯5 and an expressive stepwise line (B–A–B, C♯–D–E). Satie marks a subtle crescendo and decrescendo.
A luminous, full cadence: the music resolves softly to a pure D major harmony, bringing the first half to a peaceful resting point.
The four-bar accompaniment interlude returns (Gmaj7 alternating with Dmaj7), resetting the meditative atmosphere.
The first melody returns, identical in pitch but feeling deeper and more reflective on this second journey.
The four-measure sustained F♯4 returns, evoking an ancient Greek sculpture frozen in calm contemplation.
The second phrase of the theme unfolds over the steady pulse of the left hand.
Ascending to C♯5 and F♯5, then settling onto the long sustained E4 over the stepwise bass descent.
The rising developmental idea begins again, questioning and climbing toward D5.
The chromatic modal climb repeats, building quiet emotional tension toward the final resolution.
The second cadence takes a haunting turn: instead of F♯, Satie writes F♮. The melody drops with somber gravity through F♮5 and F♮4.
Final cadence: unlike the bright D major of bar 39, Satie concludes on a quiet, melancholic D minor chord (D–F♮–A–D). The piece vanishes into silence.

sections.label: VI
sections.name: Theme 4 · Du bout de la pensée (bars 47–54)

guide.text: The haunting opening theme in F minor with raised fourth (B♮), evoking ancient Romanian or Middle Eastern modes. Underneath, the left hand establishes the relentless "dum, chord-chord" rhythm.
Grace notes decorate the melody as it falls to B♮ and G before coming to rest on a sustained, sorrowful F4.
Theme 1 repeats in full, deepening its hypnotic, ritualistic atmosphere.
Theme 2 enters, marked "Très luisant" (very shiny). Moving to B♭ minor over low B♭ in the bass, grace notes ornament descending two-beat figures before returning to F minor.
Theme 3, inscribed "Questionnez" (questioning). A lyrical, arched phrase leaps upward (C5–D–E–F–G–B–G) and tumbles down through chromatic steps (D♭, C, B♮, A♭, G, F), repeated twice.
Theme 2 returns as a connecting ritornello, its rocking grace notes providing familiar grounding.
Theme 4, inscribed "Du bout de la pensée" (from the tip of the thought). The melody stretches out with long sustained whole notes over the unchanging left-hand pulse.
Theme 2 recurs again, maintaining the cyclical, non-linear architecture that Satie pioneered.
Theme 3 returns with the eccentric instruction "Postulez en vous-même" (wonder about yourself) and "Pas à pas" (step by step), echoing the mysterious rising question.
Theme 2 appears for the final time with the marking "Sur la langue" (on the tip of the tongue). The piece closes without a conventional cadence, simply evaporating on an open F minor chord.

debussy-clair-de-lune.title: Clair de Lune
debussy-clair-de-lune.subtitle: Claude Debussy, Suite bergamasque (1890/1905) · piano · complete

source.label: Mutopia Project edition (Mutopia-2010/12/21-1778) after E. Fromont (1905), typeset by Keith OHara

guide.text: The piece starts with a rest on the downbeat, and the soft thirds enter just after it, so you can’t hear where the 9/8 bar begins. Debussy marks it pp and con sordina (with the soft pedal).
The thirds keep stepping down. Notes tied across the beats blur the pulse even more. Look for the B𝄫 (double flat) in the left hand of bar 2: one odd note that tints the whole chord.
The melody thins to single notes and drifts downward, while the left hand moves in step beneath it.
The same shape again, an octave lower, coming to rest over an A♭ in the bass: a pause, not an ending.
The opening theme returns, now over a low D♭–A♭ bass and full G♭ chords. Same melody, much deeper colour.
Chords stack up in both hands as the phrase climbs.
The phrase peaks on B♭ and A♭ in octaves. In bar 14 the right hand plays duplets (2 notes in the time of 3) against the 9/8 pulse, then settles.
Tempo rubato: the pianist may stretch and squeeze the beat. The melody is now in octaves (F–E♭–D♭) over a low E♭ and soft repeated chords.
The answer phrase reaches up to G♭6 and falls back.
“Peu à peu cresc. et animé”: little by little louder and livelier. The left hand breaks into moving figures and the chords grow thicker.
The line climbs higher over a rising bass (D♭, then E♭).
The first climax: big rolled chords (the wavy line means arpeggiate them) high on the keyboard, then “diminuendo molto” as the sound dies away.
Un poco mosso (a little more movement): the famous flowing section. The left hand rolls arpeggios up from a low D♭ while the right hand sings above them.
The arpeggios widen to sweep over three octaves. Bar 30’s E♭ chord with G natural brightens the colour for a moment.
A sequence: the same idea over a bass that steps down A♭, G♭, F.
The melody climbs to G♭5 and B♭5. Chromatic notes in the bass (D natural, E natural) push the harmony forward.
Bars 27–28 return an octave higher, with more energy.
En animant: the key signature changes to four sharps (the same sounds as F♭ major, spelled the easy way). Marked più cresc., the melody rings out in octaves near the top of the piano.
The phrase repeats lower in a sequence, over F♯ and B chords.
The high point of the piece: parallel thirds pour down over a wide F♯ arpeggio, and the tension drains away.
Calmato (calmer): back to five flats. The left hand rocks between A♭ and E♭ (a pedal point) under quiet chords.
The chords lift to F5, then repeat; the A♭ pedal keeps everything floating.
Arpeggio echoes of bar 33’s figure, still over the pedal.
A high E♭6 rings over the left hand. In bar 50 the A natural is a chromatic signal that the opening theme is coming back.
a Tempo 1º: the opening theme returns ppp, an octave higher, but now over the flowing arpeggios from bar 27. Debussy combines his two main ideas.
The theme continues as in bars 3–4.
The single-note descent from bars 5–8, now floating over arpeggios.
Bars 9–12 return almost unchanged: the deep bass and full chords.
Thin chords over F, E♭ and A♭ in the bass: the harmony slowly turns home toward D♭.
“Morendo jusqu’à la fin”: dying away to the end. The arpeggios from bar 27 return, softer each time.
F♭ and C♭ add a last darker tint, a moment of minor, before the end.
One last arpeggio rises over five octaves to a quiet D♭ major chord.

sections.label: V
sections.name: Tempo rubato · middle section in A major (bars 39–62)

guide.text: One arpeggio shared by both hands: the left hand starts it and the right hand carries it to the top and back down, all in triplets. The gaps you see in each staff are where the other hand is playing.
Triplets against straight rhythms, with notes tied over the beat, so the pulse floats.
The line comes to rest on a long A, then steps down G♯–F♯.
The main theme: a melody falling in triplets (E–F♯–C♯–E–B…), mostly on the five notes of a pentatonic scale. Against it the left hand plays eighth notes: two against three.
The theme again, exactly as before.
The melody sinks into the tenor range and steps up slowly.
A♯ (a raised fourth) gives the line a bright, unusual colour.
G♯ and F♯ rock back and forth: a moment of stillness before the sweep returns.
The opening arpeggio comes back, now over A and F♯ harmony.
Long tied notes (D♯, B) hold while the inner line moves underneath.
A rising figure repeats, each time a step lower (a sequence). The D natural in bars 24–25 prepares a new key.
The texture drops low. Rippling figures in the left hand begin a long crescendo.
The line rises: F♯, A, D♯, then B, G♯.
A sustained A–C♯ third over a repeated turn figure.
Arpeggios climb in sixteenth notes through three octaves, getting louder all the way.
The peak on a high F♯6, then the music stops on a held E.
Tempo rubato (un peu moins vite, a little slower): the key changes to A major for the middle section, with a new, more singing melody.
The melody rises to G♯5 and B5 while the left hand supports it with chords.
The melody of bars 39–40 repeats and closes on an E chord.
Long scale-like lines climb from D3 in both hands.
The climb reaches A5, then falls back.
The rising lines repeat, ending twice on G♯5.
The middle-section melody returns, with an F natural for colour in bar 55.
The melody closes on an E chord, as in bars 43–46.
Risoluto (firmly): the key jumps to C major. Strong chords replace the flowing lines.
Chords climb step by step to B and D.
A strong melody on G5 and C5 over the chords.
The phrase repeats, but G♯ and C♯ slip in, turning it back toward E major.
Tempo 1º (original speed): back in E major, the shared arpeggio from bars 17–18 returns.
Bars 3–5 return note for note.
The main theme in triplets, as in bars 6–9.
The low, rising line from bars 10–12.
The A♯ colour and the rocking G♯–F♯ from bars 13–16.
The arpeggio sweep from bars 17–18.
New music: the melody falls in a sequence of short phrases, each a step lower.
The line keeps sinking. Bar 94 is a short 2/4 bar, which stretches the phrase before the coda.
The coda: A held as a breve (a note twice as long as a whole note) tied into the next bar while the right hand starts to climb.
A wide arpeggio sweeps up to E6 and back down.
Arpeggios climb over G♯ and B chords.
The main theme’s falling triplets, high up, as a farewell.
Rising broken figures climb octave by octave.
A high E–G♯ third rings three times, then one low E ends the piece.
